rationale: Acey (2010) uses a mixed-methods design combining 783 household surveys across 18 neighbourhoods in Lagos and Benin City with qualitative semi-structured interviews to analyze gendered community mobilisation and Hirschman's exit, voice, and loyalty responses to urban water supply failures. Multiple institutional mechanisms are co-central: community participation and mobilisation through voluntary associations such as Community Development Associations, landlord/tenant associations, and religious groups (participation_assistance, primary mechanism frame) alongside official consumer complaint/grievance channels to utilities and government ministries (review_redress), complicated by property-owner/receipt prerequisites for complaining to the Lagos Water Corporation (eligibility_status_documentation) and accountability gaps from informal private water vending competing with public utilities (regulatory_model_ownership). Empirically measured outcomes span both civic complaint/governance engagement and inability to influence sector decision-making (administrative_outcome, focal dependent variable) as well as household service intermittency, daily water quantity, potability, fetching burden (effective_access), and high vendor water expenditure (economic_access).
